comparison: Both strongly support ChatGPT's validation as a sentiment analysis tool (C2, C3, C16, C46-C48, C83, C97-C99, C105-C107, C110-C111). OpenEval emphasizes the methodological rigor including comparison with TextBlob/VADER and multiple validation approaches. Peer reviewers explicitly praise this as the 'biggest strength' and 'innovative method' with 'solid evidence.' Complete agreement on this being a well-supported contribution.

Major disagreement on interpretation. Both address inter-reviewer reliability findings (C6, C27-C31, C55-C59, C85). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to confounders (reviewer backgrounds C57, ChatGPT unreliability C58, selection bias C25/C49-C51) and inability to distinguish legitimate expert disagreement from problematic subjectivity. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting this as 'an important contribution' without questioning the causal interpretation of subjectivity.

Significant disagreement on confidence level. Both address gender-politeness findings (C8, C38-C41, C66-C68). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN citing imperfect gender inference (C92-C93), small effect size, lack of confounder controls, and inability to establish causation. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, explicitly confirming the finding as evidence of gender disparity without methodological challenge, noting it aligns with known discrimination patterns.

Fundamental disagreement. Both address female senior author findings (C10, C42-C44, C75-C82). OpenEval rates UNSUPPORTED, emphasizing the authors' own acknowledgment of likely spurious association due to collider bias (C75), selection bias undermining interpretation, and entirely speculative explanations. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the empirical finding without challenge despite acknowledged dataset limitations.

Disagreement on interpretation of null findings. Both address institutional/geographical null results (C35-C37, C61-C65). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting null results are difficult to interpret with selection bias, lack of power calculations, coarse geographical categorization, and that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the null findings as reported without raising these interpretive concerns.

Both support descriptive statistics (C4-C5, C18-C22, C25-C26, C49-C51). OpenEval notes these are straightforward descriptive results with appropriate selection bias caveats. Peer reviewers accept the findings, with Reviewer 2 noting 'well presented and informative' figures and acknowledging the pilot study limitations. Complete agreement on these being well-documented descriptive findings.

Both support acceptance time findings (C32-C34). OpenEval notes clear statistical relationships with appropriate reporting, though R² values are relatively low (14% and 7%). Peer reviewers implicitly accept these secondary analyses without comment. Agreement that these are well-supported findings, though OpenEval provides more critical context about effect sizes.

Both support the null interaction effect for gender combinations (C45). OpenEval notes this is appropriately reported but may lack power and is complicated by selection bias. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly finds the supplementary analysis 'thoughtful' and notes the pattern as 'interesting.' Agreement on accepting the finding, though OpenEval raises more interpretive cautions.

Disagreement on methodological adequacy. Both address gender categorization methods (C92-C96). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, detailing significant limitations: imperfect name-based inference, less rigorous first author verification, binary framework excluding non-binary individuals, unspecified validation subset size, and potential manual verification bias. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the Genderize approach without raising these methodological concerns.

Both support statistical methods (C100-C104). OpenEval explicitly notes appropriate use of mixed effects models, log transformation for ICC, and non-parametric tests, calling these 'sound statistical practice.' Peer reviewers implicitly accept through lack of critique. Complete agreement that statistical approaches are appropriate and well-documented.

Both support the sentiment-politeness relationship (C23-C24, C108-C109). OpenEval notes 60% variance explained indicates strong but incomplete relationship, with minor concern about polynomial choice. Peer reviewers accept without challenge. Agreement on this being well-supported, though OpenEval provides more methodological detail.

Both support dataset description and scope (C1, C13-C15, C49-C54, C88-C91). OpenEval notes internal consistency and appropriate limitation acknowledgment. Peer reviewers confirm the dataset scope, with Reviewer 1 noting 'a lot of effort in data collection.' Complete agreement on well-documented dataset with appropriate caveats.

Both support acknowledgment of study limitations (C49-C54). OpenEval emphasizes these limitations throughout multiple results as affecting interpretation. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the article now acknowledges its limitations' as pilot/proof-of-concept. Agreement that limitations are appropriately acknowledged, though OpenEval applies these more stringently in evaluating individual claims.

Partial overlap on descriptive statistics. OpenEval R7 addresses sentiment-politeness correlation (C23-C24, C108-C109) while Peer R6 includes these claims (C23-C24) within broader descriptive findings (C4-C5, C18-C26, C49-C51). Both support the statistical relationships, with peer reviewers finding figures 'well presented and informative.'
